title: From Hong Kong Phones to Solar Installations in Arusha
dek: After a year trading cheap phones from Hong Kong, a Tanzanian teenager went back to study solar power and opened a small installation business in Arusha.

story.company: Helvetic Solar Contractors (later the Helvetic Group)
story.event: Leaving a paying phone trade to study solar power and install it himself
story.summary: At 18, on a gap year, Patrick Ngowi used about $1,800 lent by his mother and a free ticket to Hong Kong to trade cheap Chinese-made phones in Tanzania, selling more than 5,000 by his count. Seeing a longer-term opportunity in solar, he studied renewable energy, opened Helvetic Solar Contractors in Arusha around 2007 and did the first installations himself. After a warehouse robbery in 2009 forced a fresh start, the company said it had installed over 2,000 systems by early 2013.
paragraphs: At eighteen, on a gap year between school and university, Patrick Ngowi had two things to start with. One was the equivalent of $1,800 from his mother, a teacher who, he later said, could not afford more. The other was a free return ticket to Hong Kong from a close family friend. For about a year he made regular trips, buying inexpensive phones from Chinese manufacturers and selling them in Tanzania to rural buyers who could spend perhaps $20 to $25. He says he sold well over 5,000.

The trade was paying. How We Made It in Africa reported that he had an annual turnover of $150,000 at 18; a later profile called the same sum profit. But it was on those Hong Kong trips, the site wrote, that he learnt what solar power could do. "I spotted the long term opportunity in solar and decided to venture into it," he told Ventures Africa in 2013. The trade needed a technical background, he said, so he studied renewable energy, concentrating on solar, at a university in China. In 2013 he put the share of Tanzanians with electricity at about 14 per cent.

He did not wait to graduate. "I opened my first company before I finished university in China," he said; he had led his own company since the age of 22, and Helvetic Solar Contractors was founded in 2007. He opened a first office in his home town, Arusha, starting with homes and small jobs. "I did all the installations myself at the time," he said. His parents, both teachers, and his siblings helped him manage the office, though business, he said, had not been "an easy swallow" for a family of academics.

In 2009 the company's warehouse was robbed, which he called "heart breaking", and according to How We Made It in Africa the team had to change its model and start from scratch. By early 2013 he said Helvetic had installed more than 2,000 small and medium solar power and water-heating systems across Tanzania, for homes, schools, clinics and UN projects, through 26 agents. Revenue figures vary: How We Made It in Africa, citing Forbes, gave $6.8 million for 2012, and profiles in 2015 and 2022 said about $8 million.

quote.text: Who progress in it makes, seems drawing back; Its even way is like a rugged track.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Leaving a phone trade that paid for a lecture hall, and then for a small office where he fitted every panel himself, could easily have looked like a step down. Laozi's verse says that real progress often looks like that, and that a sound road can feel rough underfoot.

reflection: Ngowi's phone trade worked. What he gave up for solar was not a failure but an income, and for a while the new path meant study, one office and his own hands on every installation. From outside, that can look like going backwards.

You may know something like it: work that pays steadily on one side, and on the other something slower that asks you to learn before it gives anything back. Laozi does not promise the slower road will win. He only says that progress on it often looks like retreat, so the look of it is a poor guide. On those days it is fair to judge the new work by what you are learning, not yet by what it earns.
invitation: Write down one thing you have learnt this month that you could not have learnt by doing only the work that pays. Keep the note where you will see it on a slow day.

cross_checks.claim: Before solar, Ngowi traded inexpensive Chinese-made phones in Tanzania, on trips to Hong Kong, starting with about $1,800 from his mother.
He moved from phones into solar after learning about it on those trips, and studied renewable energy at a university in China.
Helvetic Solar Contractors was founded in 2007, when Ngowi was about 22.
The first office was in Arusha.
Revenue was reported as $6.8 million for 2012 and later as about $8 million.

research_notes: Most coverage of Ngowi is profile journalism; the story leans on his own words in the 2013 Ventures Africa interview (cited from a full reprint on the Tanzanian Michuzi blog, since the original page could not be found) and the 2014 How We Made It in Africa Q&A. Conflicts: (1) First business: Ngowi and How We Made It in Africa say he sold airtime vouchers at 15; TRUE Africa (2015) says he started at 15 selling phones from China with $50. The story uses his own account (phones at 18). (2) The $1,800: Ngowi says it was a loan from his mother during his gap year, used for the phone trade; TRUE Africa says he used it after graduating to export solar products. The story uses his account. The Ventures Africa interviewer's question says he was 'nine' when given the loan, which his own answer contradicts; ignored. (3) The $150,000 at 18 is 'annual turnover' in How We Made It in Africa (2014) and 'profit' in African Leadership Magazine (2022); the story gives turnover and notes the other. (4) Where he learnt of solar: Hong Kong (How We Made It in Africa) or trips between China and Tanzania (African Leadership Magazine); the story keeps Hong Kong, which matches Ngowi's own mention of the Hong Kong ticket. (5) Revenue: $6.8m for 2012 (How We Made It in Africa citing Forbes; the Forbes article itself returns 403) against 'over $8 million' (TRUE Africa 2015) and '$8 million' (African Leadership Magazine 2022); both are given with who said what. (6) University: Wikipedia names Wenzhou University and TRUE Africa 'Denzhou University'; the story says only 'a university in China'. Founding year 2007 comes from Wikipedia; it agrees with How We Made It in Africa's 'CEO since age 22' and his January 1985 birth date. The 2009 warehouse robbery is reported only by How We Made It in Africa; the story attributes it. The figures of 2,000 systems and 26 agents are Ngowi's own claims in 2013. The 14 per cent electricity figure is his 2013 statement, placed as 'years later'. The Laozi lines are verse that Legge presents as quoted from 'the sentence-makers' within chapter 41.
